newsitem.title: UK: Suppliers dominate UK electrical retail market.
newsitem.headline: Suppliers dominate UK electrical retail market.

text.p: Suppliers call the tune in Britain's electricals retailing market, which may work against consumers' interests, according to a report on electrical retailers from retail analysts Verdict Research.
Retailers do not operate a cartel, but there is virtual price uniformity and there are no discounters in the market.

The relationship between retailers -- such as Dixons Group Plc and Comet, owned by Kingfisher Plc -- and their suppliers is already under investigation by Britain's competition watchdog the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Verdict said the MMC completed its report on April 30, but predicted it would be some weeks before its results were made public.

Verdict's own investigation found there was an unusually high degree of influence by suppliers and manufacturers on the marketplace to stabilise and maintain control of prices, and to protect profits and brand integrity.
"These are global manufacturers whose aim is to stabilise the market to generate consistent growth across a variety of outlets."
Verdict said suppliers argued that their products needed to be supported by high levels of service and suitable environments.

"If a retailer wanted to develop a low cost format, which offered consumers a trade off - functional, low key service and environments in exchange for lower prices - they would find it impossible to obtain supplies," Verdict said.
Unlike most retailers, electrical stores are not entirely free to determine their own ranges, prices and exactly how they are going to add value for customers, the report said.
"Whether the MMC is able to impose and enforce a different relationship between retailers and their suppliers remains to be seen."
And Verdict concluded this might not benefit consumers in the short run as it could lead to higher prices.

As well as the MMC uncertainty, the electrical retailers face an increase in insurance premium tax on warranties sold with electrical goods to 17.5 percent from 2.5 percent included in last year's budget.

Verdict said with most retailers generating an average eight percent of turnover from warranties, companies large or small would see their most profitable source of income come under intense pressure.
The report predicted retailers would be forced to raise prices by between one and two percent to protect margins and profits.
The tax hike would give a competitive advantage to other players in the warranty market - such as insurance firms and banks - which only face an increase in the tax to four percent from 2.5 percent.
Verdict said Dixons remained the market leader, with its market share up 27 percent in just two years to 18.8 percent. Comet remained the number two, with 6.2 percent of the market.
These two have benefited from rationalisation in the market, which has seen the demise of most of the regional electricity companies' retail chains.
